sources.citation: Heeschen, Volker. 1992. The position of the Mek languages of Irian Jaya among the Papuan languages; history, typology, and speech. Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 148(3/4): 465-488. doi:10.1163/22134379-90003146.
sources.note: p. 467 puts 'the dialects spoken in the Iluk.. valleys' (Iluk = Nipsan) in the north-western group beside the Yale language of Kosarek; p. 470: 'In Eipomek and in the dialects east of Eipomek, accent is phonemic. Angguruk places the accent on the last syllable, and the Yale language tends to place it on the last syllable.' This is said of Yale (Kosarek, kosa1249), not of Nipsan.
sources.venue: Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde

sources.note: Phonology section '[under construction]', verbal morphology 'Nothing is known'. Bibliographic value only: names the existing data as Bromley n.d. unpublished survey vocabulary (unobtained), Voorhoeve 1975: 116 (37 items), and Heeschen 1992 Yale dictionary p. 8 / some Iluk-valley forms.

sources.citation: Harimansyah, Ganjar, Tengku Syarfina & Satwiko Budiono. 2023. Pemetaan bahasa di Kabupaten Yahukimo (Language mapping in Yahukimo District). Sawerigading 29(1), June 2023. Makassar: Balai Bahasa / Badan Pengembangan dan Pembinaan Bahasa.

sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: No phonology content: location and dialectometry only ('isolek Mek Nipsan merupakan sebuah bahasa dengan persentase perbedaan berkisar 87,25%-100% jika dibandingkan dengan.. Mek Kosarek, Mek Nalca, Hubla, Dajub (Tokuni), dan Awban (Bese)').

sources.citation: Ethnologue, Nipsan [nps] (free 2016/2017 pages via the Internet Archive).
sources.note: Nothing on phonology. Alternate names Southern Jale, Yale-Nipsan; 2,500 speakers (1993 R. Doriot); Kurima sub-district west of Hmanggona; lexical similarity 78% with Kosarek Yale, 59% with Nalca; Bible portions 1982; distinct from the three Yali (Dani-family) languages.

sources.citation: Logmans, Ardjan. 2009. De Bijbel in de taal van het hart. Reformatorisch Dagblad, 8 oktober 2009 (1791 words; Digibron id tag:RD.nl,20091008:newsml_8eae79c6c71c3b085833e9e9348c72e7). Profile of ZGG language worker Alinda Paul, Nipsan (Papua).
sources.note: No phonology content. States that Alinda Paul (ZGG, sent out August 1996) had as her first tasks 'het leren en op schrift stellen van de taal' (learning the Nipsan language and committing it to writing), then setting up literacy work and supervising the New Testament translation; translation issues discussed are lexical (loanword vs. paraphrase for 'hogepriester' etc.); c. 4,500 speakers.

sources.citation: Silzer, Peter J. & Heljä Heikkinen. 1984. Index of Irian Jaya Languages. Irian: Bulletin of Irian Jaya XII. Jayapura: Universitas Cenderawasih & Summer Institute of Linguistics. Entry 314 Nipsan (Wanam; Ikliklum Yubu; Hamlo), printed p. 54 (p. 30). [First edition of the Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive description Silzer & Heikkinen-Clouse 1991.]
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: No phonology content. Gives sources 'SIL; NRC-Louwerse (p.c.)', classification, population 1,500-5,000, location, and 'NOTE: Wordlist in file: D - Steinbring - Walmak' (an unpublished UNCEN-SIL survey wordlist); no REFERENCES line, i.e. no published study of Nipsan known to the compilers in 1984.

sources.citation: Heeschen, Volker. 1978. The Mek languages of Irian Jaya with special reference to the Eipo language. Irian: Bulletin of Irian Jaya Development 7(2): 3-46. Jayapura: Universitas Cenderawasih / SIL.
sources.note: Only group-level: p. 12 'Stress seems to be partially phonemic in the east, e.g. Ok Bab 'uku fire and aha young plant of sweet potatoes, while tones are said to be phonemic in Nalca and Kosarek (Bromley 1973:15 and Rule and Cutting).' Nipsan is listed p. 7 as '(6) a: Nipsan, b: Yali, c: see map' with no data source of Heeschen's own, and placed p. 10 in the western group with Eipo, Nalca, Korapun, Kosarek; its only data are Bromley's wordlists via Voorhoeve 1975a (p. 8). No statement about Nipsan stress.
sources.venue: Irian: Bulletin of Irian Jaya Development

sources.citation: Bromley, H. Myron. 1977. The current role of missions and churches in Irian Jaya. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 3: Language, culture, society, and the modern world, 469-496. Pacific Linguistics C-40. Canberra: ANU. §7.3.3.6 The Goliath Family, p. 481.
sources.note: The tonal statement in the passage is about Hmanggona (Nalca): Murray and Joan Rule 'have done careful analysis of the phonology of the language at Nalca.. which is clearly tonal with two contrastive tonemes'; Ngalum is called a tone language. No linguistic work at Nipsan is reported; nothing on Nipsan stress or tone.
sources.venue: New Guinea area languages and language study

sources.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1975. Central and Western Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 1: Papuan languages and the New Guinea linguistic scene, 345-459. Pacific Linguistics C-38. Canberra: Australian National University. (§2.6.2.2.7 The Goliath sub-phylum-level family, pp. 398-400; §2.6.2.2.7.2 Yaly.)
sources.note: For Yaly: only cognation percentage and three pronouns (na, nu, an); 'No further data are available.' Tone statements in the same section concern other Mek varieties: Naltya 'is tonal and has two tonemes, low-rising, and high-falling' (from Bromley's phonological statement) and Korapun 'is reported to be tonal'. Nothing on Yaly/Nipsan stress or tone.
sources.venue: New Guinea area languages and language study

sources.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1975. Languages of Irian Jaya: Checklist. Preliminary classification, language maps, wordlists. Pacific Linguistics B-31. Canberra: ANU. Entry 122 'Yaly' (Goliath stock-level family, pp. 46-47) and 37-item wordlist '122. YALY (Br)' after Bromley, printed pp. 116-117 (p. 120).
sources.note: Nothing. The Yaly entry gives no dialects, villages or description (sources 'U 12, 13' only); the wordlist uses a unified orthography that is 'neither phonemic nor accurately phonetic' and marks no stress or tone.
